### Problem: GCD Arrays {#sec-gcd-p5-parity}

::: {.p-statement}
**Decide if `k` product-moves can force a shared factor.** The array `a` is every integer in
$[\,l, r\,]$. In one move you remove two elements and insert their **product** in their place
(the array shrinks by one). Can the gcd of the array be made greater than $1$ using at most
$k$ moves? Answer `t` independent test cases.

```text
[1,1], k=0            -> NO      (single element 1)
[3,5], k=1            -> NO      (a = 3,4,5)
[13,13], k=0          -> YES     (single element 13)
[4,4], k=0            -> YES
[3,7], k=4            -> YES
[4,10], k=3           -> YES
[2,4], k=0            -> NO
[1,7], k=3            -> NO
[1,5], k=3            -> YES
```

For $a = [3,4,5]$ with $k = 1$ the three possible products are $[3,20]$, $[4,15]$, $[5,12]$ -
each still has $\gcd = 1$, so the answer is NO. The whole question collapses to a **count**.

**Constraints.** $1 \le t \le 10^5$; $1 \le l \le r \le 10^9$; $0 \le k \le r - l$.
Source: [CF 1629B · GCD Arrays](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1629/B){.solved rating="800"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
To make $\gcd > 1$ it is enough (and optimal) to make every element **even**. A product is
even iff at least one factor is even, so one move can absorb a single odd number: multiply it
by any even and the even "survives" (stays even) to absorb the next odd. Thus each odd costs
exactly one move and evens are free - the answer is YES iff the number of odds in $[l, r]$ is
at most $k$. The one degenerate case is a single-element array: no move is possible and the
gcd is the element itself, so it is YES iff $l > 1$. This is @sec-gcd-a6's pigeonhole in its
purest form - a big input decided entirely by a parity count.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Count odds by walking the range.** Enumerate $l, \ldots, r$ and tally the odd values,
   then compare to $k$. The definition, viable only for tiny ranges.
2. **Closed-form parity count.** Odds in $[l,r]$ $= \lfloor (r+1)/2 \rfloor - \lfloor l/2
   \rfloor$; decide $\mathit{odd} \le k$ (with the $l = r$ special case). $O(1)$ per test case.
:::

::: {#fig-gcd-p5-parity}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["x",    "1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6", "7"],
                   ["odd?", "Y", ".", "Y", ".", "Y", ".", "Y"]],
           colors={(1, 1): "amber", (1, 3): "amber", (1, 5): "amber", (1, 7): "amber"},
           cell_w=1.0)
V.show(draw)
```

For $[\,1,7\,]$ there are four odds (amber). Each product-move absorbs at most one odd, so
$k = 3$ moves leave an odd behind and the gcd stays $1$ - the answer is NO; you would need
$k \ge 4$.

:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Walk the range and tally the odds

::: {.form-next}
Count the odd elements by literally visiting $l, l+1, \ldots, r$; a single-element range is
decided by whether that element exceeds $1$; otherwise YES iff the odd count fits in $k$.
This is the reference you trust for small inputs, but it is $O(r - l)$ and dies at $r \le 10^9$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def pa_naive(l, r, k):
    if l == r:
        return "YES" if l > 1 else "NO"
    odds = sum(1 for x in range(l, r + 1) if x % 2 == 1)
    return "YES" if odds <= k else "NO"

assert pa_naive(1, 1, 0) == "NO"
assert pa_naive(3, 5, 1) == "NO"
assert pa_naive(13, 13, 0) == "YES"
assert pa_naive(4, 4, 0) == "YES"
assert pa_naive(1, 5, 3) == "YES"
```

##### C++

```cpp
string paNaive(long long l, long long r, long long k) {
    if (l == r) return (l > 1) ? "YES" : "NO";
    long long odds = 0;
    for (long long x = l; x <= r; ++x)
        if (x % 2 == 1) odds++;
    return (odds <= k) ? "YES" : "NO";
}
```

:::

#### Closed-form parity count

::: {.form-next}
The number of odds in $[l,r]$ is $\lfloor (r+1)/2 \rfloor - \lfloor l/2 \rfloor$ - no loop
needed. Answer YES iff that count is $\le k$, except when $l = r$ (no move possible), where
the answer is YES iff $l > 1$. $O(1)$ per test case, so $t \le 10^5$ is trivial.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("parity", "count")
    assert str(final) == "YES/NO per case"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def pa_fast(l, r, k):
    if l == r:
        return "YES" if l > 1 else "NO"
    odd = (r + 1) // 2 - l // 2
    return "YES" if odd <= k else "NO"

_official = {(1, 1, 0): "NO", (3, 5, 1): "NO", (13, 13, 0): "YES", (4, 4, 0): "YES",
             (3, 7, 4): "YES", (4, 10, 3): "YES", (2, 4, 0): "NO", (1, 7, 3): "NO",
             (1, 5, 3): "YES"}
for (l, r, k), want in _official.items():
    assert pa_fast(l, r, k) == want
for _ in range(400):
    l = random.randint(1, 40); r = random.randint(l, 60); k = random.randint(0, r - l + 1)
    assert pa_fast(l, r, k) == pa_naive(l, r, k), (l, r, k)
```

##### C++

```cpp
string paFast(long long l, long long r, long long k) {
    if (l == r) return (l > 1) ? "YES" : "NO";
    long long odd = (r + 1) / 2 - l / 2;
    return (odd <= k) ? "YES" : "NO";
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time.** Rung 1 is $O(r - l)$ per case (unusable at $r \le 10^9$); rung 2 is $O(1)$ per case,
so $O(t)$ overall. **Space.** $O(1)$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **Single element.** $l = r$: no move is even possible, so the verdict is the element's own
  gcd - YES iff $l > 1$ (hence `(1,1,0) -> NO` but `(4,4,0) -> YES`).
- **Zero moves.** $k = 0$: YES only if the array already has $\gcd > 1$, i.e. no odds at all -
  a range with $l < r$ always contains an odd, so it is NO unless every element is even, which
  a length-$\ge 2$ consecutive range never is.
- **All-even impossible for $l<r$.** Two consecutive integers have opposite parity, so any
  range of length $\ge 2$ has at least one odd and at least one even - the even is always there
  to absorb an odd.

**Debug tip.** Getting a wrong verdict usually means you forgot the $l = r$ special case and
divided a one-element range into the "each odd costs a move" logic - but a single element can
never be moved, so it must be answered from $l > 1$ alone.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Thinking the move computes a gcd (the title says "GCD Arrays") - it multiplies two elements;
  the gcd is only the *goal*, checked at the end.
- Answering the single-element case as if a move could happen. With one element there is no
  pair to combine; the answer is decided by whether that element already exceeds $1$.
- Miscounting odds with `r/2 - l/2` instead of `(r+1)/2 - l/2`; the latter counts $r$ itself
  as odd when it is.
:::

**Variants.** @sec-gcd-p5-merge is the sibling "big input, forced answer" problem where a
stack folds runs instead of a count deciding parity; @sec-gcd-a6 derives the pigeonhole
"count decides it" principle this problem is built on; @sec-gcd-a3 contrasts it with a real
residue histogram.
